exam: Place Waipara an hour north of Christchurch and say why it is warmer than the plains: the Teviotdale Hills block the easterly.
Name Riesling as the signature white in every sweetness and Pinot Noir on limestone-bearing clay as the red.
Know the three nested GIs, Canterbury, North Canterbury (registered 2020) and Waipara Valley, and that the trade now says North Canterbury.
Give the two soils, Glasnevin gravels on the floor and Omihi clay on the hills, and Waikari's limestone beyond.
Name Pegasus Bay as the house, and Bell Hill and Pyramid Valley as the Waikari cult estates.
Describe the nor'wester, the hot dry föhn, as the region's own hazard.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The region's red, savoury, structured and dark-fruited from the limestone-bearing clay of Omihi and Waikari, firmer than Central Otago's.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The signature white: lime, apple and honeysuckle over taut acidity, made in a ladder from dry through off-dry to late harvest and botrytised, and long-lived.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Mineral and fine from the clay and from Waikari's limestone, barrel fermented with a light hand on new oak.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Pear and spice, off-dry and textured, a commercial staple on the gravels.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Fresh and herbal from the gravel terraces, less pungent than Marlborough's.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: A small, aromatic crop, dry to off-dry, in the cool bright autumn.

law.classification: Three registered Geographical Indications nest like Russian dolls: Canterbury for the whole east coast, North Canterbury for the northern part of it, holding the Waipara Valley and Waikari, and Waipara Valley for the valley itself. North Canterbury, filed when the register opened in July 2017, was registered on 29 June 2020. A label may use any of the three that is true for 85 per cent of its grapes, and the same share governs a stated grape or vintage. Waikari, Omihi, Glasnevin and the Canterbury Plains are addresses without registration. The atlas keeps the old course heading Canterbury / Waipara; the trade now says North Canterbury.
labels: Waipara
The valley, its river and its township; the label name of the region's fine wine.
Omihi
The limestone-bearing clay hills on the valley's eastern side, the Pinot Noir ground.
Glasnevin
The gravel terraces along the Waipara River, the Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc ground.
Nor'wester
The hot dry föhn wind off the Alps, Canterbury's own hazard.
Pegasus Bay
The bay north of Christchurch, and the name of the valley's best-known house.
tiers: Canterbury GI
The whole east coast region around Christchurch, applied for in the first intake of 2017; the broadest name.
North Canterbury GI
The northern part of Canterbury, holding the Waipara Valley and Waikari, registered on 29 June 2020; the name the trade now prefers.
Waipara Valley GI
The valley itself, the innermost of the three names; the one on most of the region's fine wine.
The 85 per cent rule
Any of the three names needs that share of the grapes from inside it; the same for a stated grape or vintage.
Addresses
Waikari, Omihi, Glasnevin, Cheviot, Banks Peninsula, the Canterbury Plains: vineyard descriptions without registration.

made.viticulture: Waipara's advantage is the hills: the Teviotdales turn away the easterly that keeps Christchurch's summers cool, so the valley gains the warmth to ripen Pinot Noir and still keeps the cold nights Riesling wants. Vines are on vertical shoot positioning, cane pruned, with crops held low on the clay hills and moderate on the gravels; the gravels are drip irrigated, the hills often dry farmed. The nor'wester is the hazard that is the region's own, a hot dry wind off the Alps that can scorch, dehydrate and strip flowers, so shelter belts and row orientation are planned around it. Frost is the plains' problem more than the valley's. The dry autumn lets Riesling hang into May for late harvest and botrytised styles at the houses that want them, and growers choose each year between a dry wine picked early and a sweeter one left out. Waikari, inland and higher on limestone, is cooler and later and farmed organically or biodynamically by its two famous estates. On the plains, vines were planted in Lincoln College's trials of 1973 (the college is now Lincoln University) and the first commercial vineyards followed in 1978 at Belfast and 1981 at Burnham, but wind and frost sent most growers north.
made.winemaking: Riesling is the region's craft: pressed gently, fermented cool in tank, often stopped with residual sugar to balance the acidity, and made in a ladder from dry through off-dry to late harvest and fully botrytised, with the best ageing a decade on their acid. Pinot Noir is hand picked, partly whole bunch at some houses, wild fermented in open tanks, raised in French oak with a modest share new, and bottled unfined: the style is savoury, structured and dark-fruited, with a firmness the limestone-bearing soils are credited with. Chardonnay from the clay and the Waikari limestone is barrel fermented with wild yeast and a restrained hand on new oak. Pinot Gris and Gewürztraminer are off-dry aromatics; Sauvignon Blanc is fresh and fermented in tank. Organic and biodynamic farming is common, several estates are certified, and screwcap is the norm.

places.name: Waipara Valley
places.note: The sheltered valley an hour north of Christchurch, first planted commercially in 1981 and the home of nearly all the region's fine wine; Riesling on the river gravels, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay on the limestone-bearing clay hills, with a long dry autumn for sweet wines.

places.name: Glasnevin gravels
places.note: The alluvial greywacke terraces along the Waipara River on the valley floor, light and free-draining, drip irrigated; Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris.

places.name: Omihi hills
places.note: The clay and limestone hills on the eastern side of the valley, water-holding and low in vigour; the Pinot Noir and Chardonnay of Greystone, Black Estate and their neighbours.

places.name: Waikari
places.note: The inland hill basin north-west of Waipara at higher altitude on chalky limestone, cooler and later, with two small estates farmed organically or biodynamically, Bell Hill and Pyramid Valley, whose Pinot Noir and Chardonnay carry the region's highest reputation.

places.name: The Canterbury Plains
places.note: The flat, stony outwash plains around Christchurch where the modern region began with Lincoln College's trials of 1973 and commercial vineyards at Belfast in 1978 and Burnham in 1981; frosty, windy and now a small share of the vineyard.

places.name: Banks Peninsula
places.note: The volcanic headland south-east of Christchurch where French settlers planted vines at Akaroa in 1840; a few small coastal vineyards today.

places.name: Cheviot
places.note: The district north of Waipara towards Kaikōura with a handful of vineyards on clay and gravel, the northern edge of North Canterbury.

producers.name: Pegasus Bay
producers.why: Planted at Waipara in the mid 1980s with a first vintage in 1991, the region's best-known house, for Riesling in every style from dry to botrytised and a structured Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Bell Hill
producers.why: A tiny Waikari estate planted on limestone from 1997 whose Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are among the country's most sought.

producers.name: Pyramid Valley
producers.why: A biodynamic Waikari estate planted from 2000 on limestone, with single-block Pinot Noir and Chardonnay of cult standing.

producers.name: Greystone
producers.why: An Omihi estate of the 2000s on the limestone-bearing clay, organic, known for Pinot Noir fermented in the vineyard and fine Riesling.

producers.name: Black Estate
producers.why: An organic Omihi estate with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from its own vineyards on the clay hills.

producers.name: Waipara Springs
producers.why: One of the valley's first vineyards, from the early 1980s, with Riesling and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Mountford
producers.why: A small Waipara hill estate known for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

terroir.climate: Cool and dry, with Waipara's rainfall around 650 millimetres and a long dry autumn; the Teviotdale Hills block the easterly sea breeze that chills the open plains, so Waipara runs warmer than Christchurch, and the nor'wester, a hot dry föhn off the Alps, can add heat and strip moisture in a day. Frost threatens the plains more than the sheltered valley.
terroir.soils: Two soils and a third beyond: the Glasnevin gravels, alluvial greywacke terraces along the Waipara River, light and free-draining, where Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc do best; the Omihi hills on the valley's eastern side, clay and limestone-rich loam over calcareous bedrock, where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are planted; and the inland Waikari basin, chalky limestone at altitude. The Canterbury Plains are stony outwash gravels with thin topsoil.
terroir.topography: A narrow valley north of the plains running north-east towards the coast, flanked by the Teviotdale Hills to the east and rising west into the Waikari hill country and the foothills of the Alps. South lie Christchurch and the flat Canterbury Plains; the volcanic hills of Banks Peninsula stand off the coast.
terroir.water: The Waipara River cut the gravel terraces; the Pacific is close but the hills hide the valley from it. Rain is low enough that the gravels use drip irrigation, while the clay hills can be dry farmed in most seasons.

traps: The atlas heading is Canterbury / Waipara; the register and the trade say North Canterbury, and Waipara Valley is the GI inside it.
Waipara is warmer than Christchurch, not cooler, because the hills block the sea breeze; the nor'wester adds heat, not cold.
Riesling, not Sauvignon Blanc, is the signature white; the region makes it from dry to botrytised.
Waikari is not in the Waipara Valley; it is the inland limestone basin to the north-west with its own two famous estates.
Pegasus Bay is a house and a bay, not a GI or a sub-region.
The 1978 and 1981 plantings were on the plains near Christchurch; Waipara's first commercial vineyard came in 1981 and the move north followed.

wines.note: Lime, green apple and honeysuckle with a nervy acidity, dry or just off-dry, with a kerosene note after five years; serve cold with Asian dishes, pork belly or fresh goat's cheese.
Apricot, marmalade and honey over piercing acidity from fruit left to hang in the dry autumn; a match for blue cheese, crème brûlée and fruit tarts.
Dark cherry, plum and dried herb with a firm, savoury tannin and earthy length from the limestone-bearing clay; serve a touch cool with lamb, duck or venison. The best keep a decade.
Citrus, white peach and a chalky, mineral line from the Omihi clay and the Waikari limestone, restrained in oak; serve cool with crayfish, chicken or a cream sauce.
Pear, quince and ginger, off-dry and gently textured; a wine for pork, smoked fish and mild spice.

exam: Place Central Otago inland in the southern South Island at 45°S and call it the country's only continental climate.
Give the terroir: schist bedrock, loess and gravel, semi-arid, hot days and cold nights, frost in any month, universal irrigation.
Name Pinot Noir as three vines in four and describe it: dark cherry, thyme, ripe tannin, generous body.

List the sub-regions and their characters: Gibbston coolest and highest, Bannockburn warm, dry and most famous, Bendigo the warmest terraces, Alexandra driest and southernmost, Wanaka lake-moderated, Cromwell and Pisa the centre.
Date the story: 1864 vines at Clyde, 1981 Gibbston Valley planted, 1987 the first commercial vintage, 1997 Felton Road's first vintage, 2022 Bannockburn GI.
Know Felton Road as the house, and Rippon, Quartz Reef and Mt Difficulty behind it.
Contrast Central Otago Pinot Noir with Martinborough's: plusher and riper against firmer and more savoury.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: About three vines in four: dark cherry, plum, wild thyme and spice with ripe tannin and generous body, from the floral, lighter Gibbston and Wanaka to the dense Bannockburn and Bendigo and the taut Alexandra.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: The second grape, pear and spice, off-dry and textured, ripening well in the dry heat.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Taut and mineral from the schist, barrel fermented with care; a small crop of growing reputation.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Lime and blossom over racy acidity, dry to off-dry, long-lived in the cold nights.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: A small crop, riper and less pungent than Marlborough's.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Aromatic and dry from a handful of sites in the cool bright autumn.

law.classification: Central Otago is a registered Geographical Indication, applied for in the register's first intake of 2017, and on 1 February 2022 Bannockburn became the first sub-region inside it to be registered as a GI of its own, the district on the south side of the Kawarau arm of Lake Dunstan. Either name on a label needs 85 per cent of the grapes from inside it, and a stated grape or vintage needs the same. Gibbston, Bendigo, Cromwell, Lowburn, Pisa, Alexandra and Wanaka are growers' names and vineyard addresses. The Waitaki Valley North Otago to the north-east is a separate registered GI, limestone country, not part of Central Otago. The law says nothing of style or yield; the sub-regional ladder a server learns is the trade's.
labels: Bannockburn
The best-known sub-region, warm and dry on the old gold sluicings south of the Kawarau, and since 2022 a GI.
Gibbston
The highest and coolest sub-region, in the Kawarau Gorge.
Bendigo
The warm north-facing terraces on Lake Dunstan's east bank under the Dunstan Mountains.
Pisa
The flats and terraces on the west bank of Lake Dunstan below the Pisa Range, north of Cromwell.
Mata-Au
The Māori name of the Clutha River, the region's great river.
Dunstan
The lake behind the Clyde Dam and the mountains above Bendigo.
tiers: Central Otago GI
The regional name, applied for in the first intake of 2017; 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the boundary.
Bannockburn GI
Registered 1 February 2022, the first sub-regional GI inside Central Otago, on the south side of the Kawarau arm of Lake Dunstan.
Sub-regional names
Gibbston, Bendigo, Cromwell, Lowburn, Pisa, Alexandra, Wanaka: addresses and growers' terms, with no registered GI of their own.
Waitaki Valley North Otago GI
A separate registered GI to the north-east on limestone, cool and tiny; not Central Otago, though Otago is in both names.
Certification
BioGro and Demeter seals are private and unusually common here; SWNZ covers nearly every vineyard.

made.viticulture: Growing here is a contest with frost, drought and sun. Vineyards are planted on north-facing slopes and terraces to catch heat and shed cold air, with wind machines, water sprinklers and, on the worst nights, helicopters to fight spring and autumn frost; drip irrigation is universal because the summer is nearly rainless; and the ultraviolet light at this latitude and altitude is strong enough that canopies are managed to shade the fruit a little rather than bare it. Vines are on vertical shoot positioning, cane pruned, planted more closely than the national average and cropped low. Pinot Noir is about three vines in four, with Dijon clones, clone 10/5 and Abel in the older blocks; Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Riesling share the rest. Harvest is late and long, from late March or April at Bendigo and Bannockburn into May in Gibbston, and a hard frost before the fruit is in is the nightmare. Rabbits, birds and the wild thyme on the hills are the local colour; biodynamic farming is unusually common, with Felton Road, Rippon, Quartz Reef and Burn Cottage among the houses farmed that way. Gold miners' water races and sluicings still mark Bannockburn's vineyards.
made.winemaking: Pinot Noir is hand picked and sorted, partly destemmed with a share of whole bunches that varies by house and year, cold soaked for several days, fermented with wild yeast in open vats with plunging, pressed off and raised ten to sixteen months in French oak with a quarter to a third new, then bottled unfined and often unfiltered under screwcap. The style is generous: dark cherry and plum, wild thyme and spice, ripe tannin and a little more alcohol than Martinborough's, with the sub-regions reading as cooler and more floral in Gibbston and Wanaka, denser at Bannockburn and Bendigo, taut at Alexandra. Pinot Gris and Riesling are fermented cool and often finished off-dry; Chardonnay is barrel fermented with care over new oak; traditional-method sparkling has had a following since the 1990s, Quartz Reef its best-known maker. Rosé from Pinot Noir is a regional staple.

places.name: Gibbston
places.note: The highest and coolest sub-region, in the Kawarau Gorge between Queenstown and Cromwell on north-facing slopes above the river, where Gibbston Valley planted in 1981 and the first commercial vintage of 1987 was made; latest picking, lighter and more floral Pinot Noir, and the region's Riesling.

places.name: Bannockburn
places.note: The most famous sub-region, warm and dry, on the old gold sluicings on the south-western shore of Lake Dunstan's Kawarau arm, north-facing; Felton Road, Mt Difficulty and Carrick make dense, dark Pinot Noir here, and the name became a registered GI on 1 February 2022.

places.name: Cromwell and the Pisa flats
places.note: The centre of the region, the town at the junction of the Clutha and Kawarau and the terraces and flats running north along Lake Dunstan's west bank below the Pisa Range; warm, the largest planted area, with Lowburn and Pisa as its vineyard names.

places.name: Lowburn
places.note: The lakeside flats just north of Cromwell, warm and early, with some of the region's larger plantings.

places.name: Pisa
places.note: The terraces further north under the Pisa Range on the lake's west bank, with several estates on the warm flats and slopes.

places.name: Bendigo
places.note: The east bank of Lake Dunstan under the Dunstan Mountains, the warmest terraces in the region on north-facing slopes above an old gold mine; Quartz Reef and Prophet's Rock grow dense, structured Pinot Noir.

places.name: Alexandra
places.note: The southernmost and driest sub-region down the Clutha, the most continental of all with hot days and the coldest nights; Black Ridge planted in 1981 and the Pinot Noir is taut, bright and fine-boned.

places.name: Wanaka
places.note: The northernmost sub-region on the shores of Lake Wanaka, higher and moderated by the water, where Rippon's lakeside trials of the 1970s make it among the region's oldest vineyards; floral, elegant Pinot Noir and Riesling.

places.name: Lake Hayes and Queenstown
places.note: A few vineyards on the lake between Queenstown and Gibbston, cool and scenic, the region's tourist face.

producers.name: Felton Road
producers.why: Planted at Bannockburn in the early 1990s with a first vintage in 1997, biodynamic, with Block 3, Block 5, Calvert and Cornish Point Pinot Noirs: the region's benchmark.

producers.name: Rippon
producers.why: The lakeside Wanaka estate whose trials began in the 1970s and whose commercial vineyard dates from the 1980s, biodynamic and dry farmed; floral Pinot Noir and Riesling.

producers.name: Mt Difficulty
producers.why: Founded at Bannockburn in the 1990s, a large house whose single-vineyard Pinot Noirs map the sub-region's terraces.

producers.name: Quartz Reef
producers.why: Founded in 1996, with its vineyard at Bendigo, biodynamic, with the region's leading traditional-method sparkling and a dense Bendigo Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Gibbston Valley
producers.why: Planted in 1981 in the Kawarau Gorge, among the first wineries of the modern region and maker of one of the first commercial vintages in 1987.

producers.name: Two Paddocks
producers.why: An estate with vineyards in Gibbston and Alexandra whose Pinot Noirs show both sub-regions in one cellar.

producers.name: Burn Cottage
producers.why: A biodynamic estate at Lowburn below the Pisa Range, planted in 2003, whose Pinot Noir is among the region's most refined.

producers.name: Prophet's Rock
producers.why: A Bendigo estate on the high terraces making structured Pinot Noir and fine Pinot Gris and Riesling.

producers.name: Valli
producers.why: A house that bottles Pinot Noir from several sub-regions separately, Gibbston, Bannockburn and Bendigo among them, and teaches the differences in a flight.

terroir.climate: Continental, the only one in the country: a semi-arid basin climate behind the mountains with rainfall as low as 350 millimetres at Alexandra, hot clear summer days, cold nights, dry bright autumns and hard winters. The diurnal swing is the region's engine, ripening sugar by day and holding acid and aroma by night, and frost can strike in any month.
terroir.soils: Schist is the bedrock of the whole region, and the soils are its products: wind-blown loess, glacial outwash and river gravels, old gold-bearing alluvium at Bannockburn, with little organic matter and low fertility. They drain fast and hold little water, so irrigation is a condition of growing anything.
terroir.topography: Basins and gorges carved by the Clutha and Kawarau rivers through the schist ranges: the Cromwell Basin at the centre holding Lake Dunstan, with Bannockburn on its south-western shore, Lowburn and Pisa on the west bank and Bendigo on the east; the Kawarau Gorge running west to Gibbston and Queenstown; Alexandra down the Clutha to the south; Wanaka on its lake to the north. Vineyards sit high for New Zealand, on north-facing slopes and terraces.
terroir.water: Lake Dunstan, filled behind the Clyde Dam in the early 1990s, moderates the Cromwell Basin; Lake Wanaka does the same for its shore. The Clutha and Kawarau rivers cut the basins and supply the irrigation every vineyard needs.

traps: Central Otago is continental; every other New Zealand region is maritime. The exam's favourite exception.
Bannockburn is a GI since 2022; Gibbston, Bendigo, Alexandra and Wanaka are not, whatever a label suggests.
The Waitaki Valley is North Otago, a separate GI on limestone; it is not a Central Otago sub-region.
Gibbston is the coolest sub-region, Bendigo and Bannockburn the warmest; Alexandra is the driest and most continental, not the warmest.
The region's first commercial vintage was 1987, not the 1864 vines at Clyde and not Felton Road's 1997.
Lake Dunstan is a reservoir of the early 1990s, not a natural lake; Wanaka and Hayes are natural.
Schist is the rock; limestone belongs to Waikari and the Waitaki, greywacke to Marlborough and Hawke's Bay.

wines.note: Dark cherry, plum, wild thyme and spice with ripe, round tannin and a little more alcohol than Martinborough's, generous and immediate but able to age ten years; serve a touch cool with duck, lamb, venison or mushrooms.
Pear, quince and ginger, off-dry and textured, with the acidity of cold nights; a wine for pork, smoked fish and mild spice.
Lime, green apple and blossom over racy acidity, dry to off-dry, kerosene after a few years; serve cold with Asian food and fresh cheeses.
Citrus and white peach with a flinty, mineral edge from the schist and restrained oak; serve cool with crayfish or roast chicken.
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay bottle fermented by a handful of houses, red apple and brioche with crisp acidity; an aperitif and a match for fried food.
Strawberry and red cherry, dry and fresh, pressed early from Pinot Noir; a summer wine for salmon, salads and charcuterie.

exam: Place Gisborne on the North Island's east coast around Poverty Bay, north of Hawke's Bay, and say why it is warm, wet and early.
Name Chardonnay as the lead grape and Gewürztraminer as the historic speciality, with Pinot Gris, Chenin Blanc and Viognier behind.
Explain the soils, deep fertile alluvium from the Waipaoa, and why vigour and autumn rain shape the viticulture.
Know Millton as the organic and biodynamic pioneer and Matawhero as the Gewürztraminer name.
At Advanced, name the sub-areas, Ormond, Patutahi, Manutuke and Hexton, and the role of the region in bulk and sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The region's grape: ripe, soft and peachy from the flats for the national blends and the sparkling base, fuller and barrel fermented from the hill edges, with a buttery breadth the cooler regions do not give.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Lychee, rose and ginger, oily and usually just off-dry; the wine that made the region's name in the 1970s and 1980s.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Off-dry and textured in the Alsace manner, ripening easily in the warm season.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: A Loire-minded speciality at the biodynamic houses, dry to sweet, botrytis welcomed, long-lived.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot and honeysuckle, full and soft, a small crop that likes the warmth.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The main red, soft, plummy and early drinking from the plains.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grown for volume and blending, riper and rounder than Marlborough's, without the pungency.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Picked early for the sparkling base rather than grown for a still red.

law.classification: Gisborne is a registered Geographical Indication, one of the regional names applied for when the register opened in July 2017 under the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006. The GI draws a boundary and nothing else: no grape list, no yield, no panel. A wine that says Gisborne must take 85 per cent of its grapes from inside it, and the same share applies to a stated variety or vintage. Sub-areas such as Ormond, Patutahi and Manutuke are vineyard addresses with no registered status. Organic and biodynamic claims rest on private certification, BioGro and Demeter, and Millton's organic certification of 1989 was the country's first.
labels: Tairāwhiti
The Māori name for the Gisborne district, the coast upon which the sun shines across the water.
Poverty Bay
The bay the city sits on, Cook's name of 1769; some labels and the local trade still use it.
Chardonnay capital
The region's own slogan for its most planted grape, a claim of style and volume, not a classification.
tiers: New Zealand (GI)
The national origin a multi-region blend carries; Gisborne Chardonnay disappears into many of them.
Gisborne GI
The regional name, applied for in the first intake of 2017; 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the boundary.
Vineyard names
Ormond, Ormond Valley, Patutahi, Manutuke, Hexton, Matawhero: addresses on a label, not registered GIs.
Certification
BioGro organic and Demeter biodynamic seals are private; SWNZ is the industry's sustainability programme.

made.viticulture: Vigour is the enemy on the flats: a vine in deep wet loam grows canes faster than fruit, so the region's trellises are divided and open, Scott Henry and other split canopies, with leaf plucking and shoot thinning to let air and light into the fruit zone before the humid weeks of February and March. Harvest comes early by New Zealand standards, often from late February or early March for the sparkling base and Chardonnay, which also beats the autumn storms. The big companies built Gisborne on contract growers and machine harvesting, and much of its Chardonnay still goes into national blends and the sparkling lines; the estates that stayed favoured the better-drained hill edges, Ormond among them, and lower crops. Phylloxera is present, so vines are grafted. Millton, founded in 1984, was certified organic in 1989, the first estate in the country to be so, and went on to biodynamics, which shows that the climate can be managed without synthetic sprays when the canopy is right.
made.winemaking: Commercial Chardonnay is pressed, settled and fermented cool in tank, often with a portion in older oak and a soft malolactic, then blended and bottled young under screwcap for a round, peachy wine. The serious bottlings are barrel fermented on their lees with a share of new French oak, wild or cultured, stirred and held nine to twelve months, and they keep a buttery breadth the cooler regions lack. Gewürztraminer is picked ripe and fermented cool to hold its rose and lychee, usually dry to just off-dry, with the best left on skins briefly for texture. Chenin Blanc is made in the Loire manner at the biodynamic houses, in old oak with some residual sugar in sweeter years and botrytis welcomed. Sparkling base is picked early, pressed whole and sent to the traditional-method or tank-method lines of the big companies. Merlot is destemmed, fermented warm and given a short time in used oak for early drinking.

places.name: Ormond and the Ormond Valley
places.note: The north-western corner where the valley narrows towards the hills, planted since Friedrich Wohnsiedler's vineyard of 1921; lighter soils on the valley sides give the region's more structured Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer.

places.name: Patutahi
places.note: Inland to the west of the city on heavier soils with more clay than the flats; a long-established vineyard district, known for Gewürztraminer and Chardonnay, whose name Montana gave to an estate Gewürztraminer.

places.name: Manutuke
places.note: The southern end of the plain near the coast, on heavy alluvial soils; Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer and Chenin Blanc from the biodynamic houses.

places.name: Hexton
places.note: The hills on the northern edge of the city, older soils with better drainage than the flats; small plantings of Chardonnay and aromatic whites.

places.name: Matawhero
places.note: A locality west of the city on the Waipaoa flats, and the name of the estate whose Gewürztraminer in the 1970s and 1980s first gave Gisborne a fine wine reputation.

places.name: The Waipaoa flats
places.note: The deep, fertile river plain where the big companies' contract vineyards grow Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and the sparkling base by machine; vigorous, high-yielding and the source of most of the region's volume.

producers.name: Millton Vineyards and Winery
producers.why: Founded 1984 at Manutuke, the country's first certified organic estate and a biodynamic pioneer, famed for Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay and Viognier from its hill vineyard.

producers.name: Matawhero
producers.why: The estate whose Gewürztraminer made Gisborne's name in the 1970s and 1980s, revived under new ownership in the 2000s.

producers.name: TW Wines
producers.why: A small grower-owned Gisborne estate making Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer and Viognier from its own vineyards.

producers.name: Lindauer
producers.why: The sparkling brand launched by Montana in 1981 and built on Gisborne base wine, the bottle that put New Zealand fizz in every supermarket.

producers.name: Villa Maria
producers.why: One of the national houses that has long drawn Chardonnay and aromatic whites from Gisborne growers for its regional ranges.

terroir.climate: Warm and sunny for New Zealand, with a long growing season that starts early; rainfall is around a metre a year and part of it falls in autumn, when ex-tropical cyclones can arrive from the north-east. Humidity is high, so botrytis and downy mildew press on a vigorous canopy, and the grower's calendar is built around getting fruit in before the storms.
terroir.soils: Deep alluvial silts and clay loams laid down by the Waipaoa River and its tributaries across the flat Poverty Bay plains: fertile, water-holding and vigorous. Patutahi, inland to the west, carries heavier soils with more clay; the hill edges at Ormond and Hexton carry older soils with better drainage than the flats, and the slopes there give the region's more concentrated fruit.
terroir.topography: A flat river plain opening onto the crescent of Poverty Bay, ringed by low hills: the Ormond Valley to the north-west, the Hexton hills to the north, Patutahi inland to the west and Manutuke to the south. The ranges of the East Cape stand behind and take the brunt of the westerlies.
terroir.water: The Waipaoa River built the plain and still floods it; the Pacific on Poverty Bay keeps the climate maritime and brings the autumn rain. Drainage rather than irrigation is the grower's water problem on the heavy flats.

traps: Gisborne is north of Hawke's Bay, not south; the atlas order runs Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Wairarapa down the east coast.
Chardonnay, not Sauvignon Blanc, is the region's grape; the Sauvignon grown here goes into blends.
The region was the country's Müller-Thurgau bulk engine in the 1970s; the course note's Chardonnay is the story since the 1980s.
Poverty Bay is a bay and an old name, Tairāwhiti the Māori district name, Gisborne the GI.
The weather risk is autumn rain from the tropics, not spring frost; Gisborne is rarely frosted.

wines.note: Peach, melon and a soft, creamy breadth, with modest acidity and a touch of oak at the better houses. Serve cool rather than cold, with roast chicken, crayfish or a cream sauce; drink within five years.
Lychee, rose petal and ginger, oily on the palate, usually just off-dry; the sweetness is a match for spiced dishes, pork with fruit and washed-rind cheese.
Quince, honey and beeswax over firm acidity, dry to gently sweet depending on the year; it keeps a decade and suits river fish, pork and goat's cheese.
Early-picked Chardonnay and Pinot Noir go into the big companies' sparkling lines, Lindauer the most famous; soft, fruity and brioche-light, an aperitif rather than a vintage Champagne.
wines.style: Gisborne sparkling base and Méthode Traditionnelle

wines.note: Plum and soft tannin, medium in body, drunk young with roast lamb or a burger; it is the region's house red, not a cellar wine.

exam: Place Hawke's Bay on the North Island's east coast between Gisborne and the Wairarapa, with Napier and Hastings, and call it the warmest region of size.
Tell the Gimblett Gravels story: the Ngaruroro's flood of 1867, greywacke stones, low fertility, drip irrigation, a trademark on a soil boundary from 2001.
Give the grapes by role: Chardonnay the white, Merlot the leading red, Syrah the signature, Cabernet Sauvignon for the warm years.
Describe the Syrah as cool-climate, white pepper and violets, nearer the northern Rhône than Barossa.
Know Mission Estate (1851) as the oldest winery and Te Mata's Coleraine (from 1982) as the benchmark blend.
At Advanced, name the Bridge Pa Triangle, Havelock North, Te Awanga and Esk Valley and what each grows.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Among the most planted grapes and the region's finest white: barrel fermented, ripe stone fruit with a struck-match edge and enough acidity to age a decade.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted red because it ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon; plum and cocoa, it leads most of the region's Bordeaux blends.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Small in area and the region's signature: white pepper, violet and raspberry, medium-bodied and fresh, nearer the northern Rhône than Barossa, best from the Gimblett Gravels and the Bridge Pa Triangle.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Needs the gravels and a warm year to ripen; leads the blend then, with blackcurrant and cedar, and supports Merlot otherwise.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Perfume and freshness in the blends, occasionally bottled alone.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Colour and dark fruit for the blends; ripens well on the stones.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Riper and rounder than Marlborough's, sometimes oak fermented, grown mostly on the fertile silts.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Off-dry and generous from the plains, a commercial staple.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Grown on the cool coast at Te Awanga and in Central Hawke's Bay rather than on the warm gravels.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: A small crop, bottled alone or co-fermented in a dash with Syrah as in Côte-Rôtie.

law.classification: Hawke's Bay is a registered Geographical Indication, applied for when the register opened in July 2017 and registered on 26 February 2018, and the rule it carries is origin only: 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the line, and 85 per cent for a stated grape or vintage. The Gimblett Gravels Winegrowing District is not a GI; it is a trademark held by a growers' association, which drew it in 2001 on a soil boundary, the gravel bed of the old Ngaruroro, so a wine may use the name only if its grapes grew on those stones. The Bridge Pa Triangle is likewise a growers' name. Central Hawke's Bay, to the south, is a registered GI of its own, entered on 28 January 2019; Havelock North, Te Awanga and Esk Valley are addresses. Nothing in law ranks a vineyard or sets a yield.
labels: Gimblett Gravels
The old riverbed district; the words on a label mean the grapes grew on the stones inside the trademarked boundary.
Coleraine
Te Mata Estate's Cabernet-led blend from Havelock North, first made in 1982 and named after a family home beside its vineyard.
Syrah
The word on almost every label here rather than Shiraz: a cool, peppery, Rhône-leaning style.
Heretaunga
The Māori name of the plains between Napier and Hastings where the vineyards lie.
Hawke Bay
The body of water; the region, with its apostrophe, is Hawke's Bay.
tiers: New Zealand (GI)
The national origin; a Hawke's Bay red blended with Marlborough fruit falls back to it.
Hawke's Bay GI
The regional name, applied for in the first intake of 2017; 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the boundary.
Central Hawke's Bay GI
A local GI for the cooler hill country south of the plains, registered on 28 January 2019; small plantings.
Gimblett Gravels Winegrowing District
A trademark of the growers' association, drawn in 2001 on the boundary of the gravel soils; a soil-defined district, and not a GI.
Bridge Pa Triangle
A growers' association name for the red metal soils west of Hastings; a vineyard address in law.
Addresses
Havelock North, Te Awanga, Esk Valley, Bay View, Mangatahi: true statements with no registration.

made.viticulture: The region grows the Bordeaux grapes and Syrah where New Zealand's cool, wet climate would normally refuse them, and it does so by choosing soil over site: the Gimblett Gravels and the Bridge Pa Triangle lie inland, away from the sea breeze, on stones that shed water and give back the day's heat to the fruit zone after dark. Vines there are drip irrigated, planted closer than on the plains and trained to vertical shoot positioning with the fruit exposed; crops are held low because the soil gives little. Frost is the spring hazard on the inland flats, fought with wind machines and water; vigour is the hazard on the deep silts near the rivers, where the big companies grow Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay by machine. Chardonnay ripens anywhere on the plain; Merlot is the most planted red because it finishes earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, which needs the gravels and a warm year. Syrah was revived in the 1980s and the first modern commercial bottling came from the 1989 vintage; it is picked for pepper and perfume, not jam. The Gimblett Gravels nearly became a quarry in the 1980s before growers won the land for vines.
made.winemaking: The Bordeaux reds are destemmed, fermented warm with pump-overs or punch-downs, pressed and raised for twelve to twenty months in French oak, a third or less new at most houses, and blended across the varieties and the plain's soils; Merlot usually leads, Cabernet Sauvignon leads from the gravels in a warm year, Cabernet Franc and Malbec season the blend. Syrah is handled as in the northern Rhône: some whole bunches, a gentle extraction, at some houses a small dash of Viognier co-fermented, and used oak so that white pepper, violet and raspberry stay in front. Chardonnay is barrel fermented, wild at many houses, with lees stirring and a partial or full malolactic, and the best bottlings are built to age ten years. Sauvignon Blanc here is riper and rounder than Marlborough's and sometimes sees oak. Most wine is bottled under screwcap, though some flagship reds keep cork.

places.name: Gimblett Gravels
places.note: The stony old bed of the Ngaruroro River west of Hastings, left dry by the flood of 1867 and nearly quarried in the 1980s; low in fertility, warm by day, drip irrigated, it ripens Syrah, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon as few places in the country can. The district is a growers' trademark drawn on the soil boundary since 2001.

places.name: Gimblett Road
places.note: The road that gave the district its name, where the first vineyards went in on the stones in the 1980s.

places.name: Bridge Pa Triangle
places.note: The warm district south-west of Hastings around the village of Bridge Pa, on the reddish red metal soils over deep gravel; it holds a little more water than the Gimblett and gives softer, more aromatic Syrah and Merlot.

places.name: Havelock North
places.note: The town and its hills south-east of Hastings below Te Mata Peak, where Te Mata Estate's vines have grown since the 1890s on clay slopes over sandstone and limestone; the home of Coleraine and the region's oldest fine wine tradition.

places.name: Te Awanga and the coast
places.note: The cool coastal strip south of Napier towards Cape Kidnappers, where the sea breeze slows ripening; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc rather than the Bordeaux grapes.

places.name: Esk Valley and Bay View
places.note: The northern end of the region above Napier, a small warm valley running to the coast with old plantings of Chardonnay and the Bordeaux grapes.

places.name: Taradale and the Napier plains
places.note: The home of Mission Estate, founded 1851 and long settled at Taradale, and of Church Road's cellars, dating from 1897; silt and gravel soils growing Chardonnay, Merlot and Syrah.

places.name: Mangatahi
places.note: River terraces on the upper Ngaruroro inland to the west, cooler and higher than the plains, with gravels suited to Chardonnay and aromatic whites.

places.name: Central Hawke's Bay
places.note: The hill country south of the plains around Waipawa and Waipukurau, cooler and later, with Riesling, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc in small plantings; a registered GI of its own since 2019.

producers.name: Te Mata Estate
producers.why: The Havelock North house with vines from the 1890s, maker of Coleraine since 1982, the Bullnose Syrah and the Elston Chardonnay: the region's benchmark for age-worthy wine.

producers.name: Craggy Range
producers.why: Founded in 1997 at Havelock North, with Le Sol Syrah and the Merlot-led Sophia from its Gimblett Gravels vineyard and a Te Muna Road vineyard in Martinborough for Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Villa Maria
producers.why: The national house founded in Auckland in 1961, a large grower in Hawke's Bay and Marlborough with reserve reds from the gravels.

producers.name: Mission Estate
producers.why: Founded by the Marist fathers in 1851 and the country's oldest working winery, long settled at Taradale.

producers.name: Trinity Hill
producers.why: Founded 1993 with a Gimblett Gravels vineyard; its Homage Syrah helped define the region's Rhône-leaning style.

producers.name: Stonecroft
producers.why: The small estate whose 1989 Syrah was modern New Zealand's first commercial bottling of the grape, from vines planted in the 1980s.

producers.name: Church Road
producers.why: The Taradale cellars founded in 1897, home of the Tom red blend and a museum of the region's early winemaking.

producers.name: Elephant Hill
producers.why: A Te Awanga estate of the 2000s whose coastal Chardonnay and Syrah show the cool side of the region.

terroir.climate: Warm maritime, the warmest of New Zealand's larger regions, with long sunshine hours and warm summers; the Kaweka and Ruahine ranges to the west shelter it from the westerlies and much of their rain, so the season is drier than Gisborne's. Nights are cool, spring frost threatens the inland plains, and rain from the east can arrive at vintage.
terroir.soils: The Heretaunga Plains are the fans of three rivers, and a short walk crosses deep fertile silt, sandy loam and bare greywacke gravel. The Gimblett Gravels are the old bed of the Ngaruroro, left dry by the flood of 1867: stones with little silt, low fertility, warm by day and poor at holding water. The Bridge Pa Triangle carries the reddish soils growers call red metal, older alluvium over gravel that holds water better; the hills of Havelock North carry clay loams over sandstone and limestone.
terroir.topography: A broad coastal plain between Napier and Hastings, backed by hill country rising to the ranges, with the Te Mata Peak hills at Havelock North and the coast curving round Hawke Bay to Cape Kidnappers. Inland river terraces at Mangatahi and the cooler, higher Central Hawke's Bay lie to the south-west and south.
terroir.water: Three rivers, the Ngaruroro, the Tutaekuri and the Tukituki, shaped the plain and its soils; the Pacific at Hawke Bay cools the coast at Te Awanga and Bay View. The gravels need drip irrigation from the aquifer beneath the plain.

traps: Gimblett Gravels is a trademark, not a GI: a district drawn on a soil boundary rather than a registered line.
Merlot, not Cabernet Sauvignon, is the most planted red; Cabernet needs the stones and a warm year.
Hawke's Bay holds the oldest winery and is the second largest region; Marlborough is far larger and far younger.
Hawke's Bay Syrah is peppery and medium-bodied; a jammy description points to Australia.
Hawke Bay is the water, Hawke's Bay the region; the apostrophe belongs on the label.
The 1867 flood moved the Ngaruroro, not the Tukituki or the Tutaekuri; the three rivers are easy to mix.

wines.note: White pepper, violets, raspberry and black cherry over fine tannin, medium-bodied at moderate alcohol; serve just below room temperature with lamb, duck or a peppercorn steak. The best keep ten years and more.
Plum, blackcurrant, cedar and dried herb with firm, ripe tannin from the stones; Merlot leads in most years, Cabernet Sauvignon in the warm ones. Decant a young one and serve with beef or venison.
wines.style: Gimblett Gravels Merlot and Cabernet blend

wines.note: White peach, grapefruit and a smoky, struck-match note from barrel fermentation, with a creamy lees texture and fresh acidity; serve cool with crayfish, roast chicken or a mushroom risotto.

The region's Bordeaux blend of longest standing, Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Cabernet Franc from the Havelock North hills, made since 1982; cedar, blackcurrant and graphite, built for fifteen years.
Riper than Marlborough's, stone fruit and lime over a soft herbal edge, sometimes with a share fermented in oak; a wine for grilled fish, asparagus and goat's cheese.

exam: Place Marlborough at the north-eastern tip of the South Island around Blenheim and give its share: more than two thirds of the country's vineyard.
Date the story: Montana 1973, the first Sauvignon Blanc 1975, Hunter's in London 1986, Cloudy Bay's first vintage 1985, Deutz 1988.
Describe the style and its chemistry: pyrazines for the green notes, thiols for the passionfruit and boxwood, cool reductive winemaking under screwcap.
Contrast the Wairau and the Awatere: stony, sunny and tropical against higher, windier, cooler and greener, a fortnight later.
Know the Southern Valleys as the clay Pinot Noir country and name the five.
Give Appellation Marlborough Wine as a private seal from 2018 with its 100 per cent rule, and the GI's 85 per cent rule beneath it.
At Advanced, name Rapaura, Dillons Point, Renwick, Seddon and Blind River and say what each gives.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The region's grape and the country's: pungent passionfruit, gooseberry, grapefruit and cut grass, dry, unoaked and bottled young under screwcap; greener and more saline from the Awatere, riper and more tropical from the lower Wairau. A wild-ferment, oak-aged school makes a textured version.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The second grape, from the clay of the Southern Valleys: red cherry, raspberry and spice, lighter and softer than Martinborough's, and the base of the region's sparkling with Chardonnay.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Taut and citrus-led, barrel fermented at the better houses, with a flinty edge; also the sparkling partner of Pinot Noir.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Pear and spice, off-dry and textured, a large commercial crop.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Dry to sweet, lime and honeysuckle, and botrytised in the years the fungus comes; long-lived.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Aromatic, dry to off-dry, a small crop of old standing.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: A recent arrival suited to the cool dry season, peppery and fresh.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: Planted since the 2010s for its saline freshness; a small but growing crop.

law.classification: Marlborough is a registered Geographical Indication, applied for when the register opened in July 2017, and in law it is a boundary and an 85 per cent rule: that share of the grapes from inside it for the name, and the same for a stated grape or vintage. The Wairau Valley, the Awatere Valley and the Southern Valleys are growers' names and vineyard addresses, not registered GIs. Above the law sits Appellation Marlborough Wine, a growers' certification launched in 2018: every grape from Marlborough, bottled in New Zealand, from vineyards certified sustainable. Its seal is a promise, not a tier. Méthode Marlborough is a trade group's mark for the region's traditional-method sparkling.
labels: Wairau
The main valley and river; a label naming it means the flat, stony heart of the region.
Awatere
The southern valley over the Wither Hills: cooler, windier, greener, more saline.
Southern Valleys
Brancott, Omaka, Fairhall, Waihopai and Ben Morven, the clay side valleys where Pinot Noir grows.
Rapaura
A stony stretch of the Wairau floor north of Blenheim, along the Rapaura Road some call the Golden Mile.
Te Koko
Cloudy Bay's wild-ferment, oak-aged Sauvignon Blanc, named for the Māori name of the bay.
Brancott
The Southern Valley where Montana planted in 1973, and the name the Montana brand later took.
Cloudy Bay
The bay Cook named in 1770 and the house whose 1985 vintage made the region famous.
tiers: New Zealand (GI)
The national origin; a Sauvignon Blanc stretched with fruit from another region falls back to it.
Marlborough GI
The regional name, applied for in the first intake of 2017; 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the boundary.
Sub-valley names
Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley, Southern Valleys, Rapaura, Blind River, Kekerengu: addresses and growers' terms, with no registered GI of their own.
Appellation Marlborough Wine
A private seal from 2018: 100 per cent Marlborough grapes, bottled in New Zealand, sustainably certified vineyards.
Méthode Marlborough
A producers' group mark for traditional-method sparkling made wholly in the region.

made.viticulture: This is vineyard farming at a scale no other New Zealand region approaches: flat valley floor, long straight rows on vertical shoot positioning, four-cane pruning for Sauvignon Blanc to carry a generous crop, drip irrigation from the aquifer on stones that hold nothing, and machine harvest, mostly at night, so that cool fruit reaches the press within hours. Shade in the canopy raises the green methoxypyrazines and sun lowers them, so leaf plucking and row orientation are stylistic decisions as much as disease control. Spring frost is the great hazard on the valley floor, fought with wind machines and helicopters; wind at flowering cuts the Awatere's crop, and drought is the summer risk there, with drip water the answer. Yields for commercial Sauvignon Blanc are high by fine wine standards and the fruit still tastes of the place, which is the region's gift. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay go to the clay of the Southern Valleys, where crops are lower and picking is by hand. Leafroll virus and trunk disease are the long-term worries of a vineyard planted fast in the 1990s and 2000s. Sustainable Winegrowing certification is close to universal.
made.winemaking: The classic Sauvignon Blanc is made to protect and release aroma: machine-picked fruit with a little skin contact in the harvester bin, which raises the thiol precursors, gentle pressing with sulphur dioxide and ascorbic acid against oxidation, cold settling, a cool fermentation at around twelve to sixteen degrees with selected yeasts chosen for thiol release, no malolactic, no oak, a few grams of residual sugar in the commercial bottlings to round the acidity, and early bottling under screwcap. The aromas are the pyrazines (capsicum, cut grass, tomato leaf) and the thiols (passionfruit, grapefruit, boxwood), with the Awatere greener and the lower Wairau more tropical. A second school ferments Sauvignon Blanc with wild yeast in old barrels and gives it lees and time, Cloudy Bay's Te Koko, Greywacke's Wild Sauvignon and Dog Point's Section 94 among them. Pinot Noir is cold soaked, wild fermented and raised in French oak; Chardonnay is barrel fermented; Riesling is made dry to sweet and botrytised in the years the fungus comes. Traditional-method sparkling from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay has a record going back to the Deutz Marlborough Cuvée joint venture of 1988 and Cloudy Bay's Pelorus.

places.name: Wairau Valley
places.note: The broad flat valley of the Wairau River between the Richmond Range and the Wither Hills, the first planted and still the largest part of the region; stony and free-draining near Rapaura and Renwick, deeper and more fertile towards the coast.

places.name: Rapaura
places.note: Stony ground on the valley floor north of Blenheim along Rapaura Road, which some call the Golden Mile; low vigour, early ripening, ripe tropical Sauvignon Blanc, and the home of Cloudy Bay and its neighbours.

places.name: Renwick and the upper Wairau
places.note: The drier, warmer inland end of the valley west of Blenheim, with gravel and silt; many of the mid-sized estates are here.

places.name: Dillons Point and the lower Wairau
places.note: The deep silt loams near the river mouth east of Blenheim, where the water table is high and the fruit is loudest, most tropical and highest yielding.

places.name: Southern Valleys
places.note: The side valleys on the southern flank of the Wairau, Brancott, Omaka, Fairhall, Waihopai and Ben Morven, on clay-bound loess over gravel; cooler, water-holding, and the region's Pinot Noir and Chardonnay country, with Montana's 1973 planting at Brancott.

places.name: Brancott
places.note: The valley where Montana planted the first vines of the modern region in 1973 and which gave the company's brand its name.

places.name: Omaka and Fairhall
places.note: Clay slopes with the region's best-known Pinot Noir vineyards, hand picked and cropped low.

places.name: Waihopai
places.note: The westernmost of the side valleys, higher and drier, with gravel and clay.

places.name: Awatere Valley
places.note: The valley south of the Wither Hills around Seddon, higher, cooler, windier and drier than the Wairau, on loess terraces over gravel; later picking and a greener, more herbal, saline Sauvignon Blanc with tomato leaf and blackcurrant leaf, and fine Riesling and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Seddon
places.note: The valley's township and the centre of its vineyards, planted on the terraces above the river.

places.name: Blind River
places.note: A small, dry and exposed valley near the coast south-east of Seddon, towards Lake Grassmere, grouped with the Awatere.

places.name: Kekerengu and the South Coast
places.note: The coastal strip south of the Awatere towards Kaikōura, cool and exposed vineyards, with a small crop of Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Blenheim
places.note: The region's town at the junction of the Wairau and its side valleys, the base of most wineries and the place whose sunshine record the region quotes.

producers.name: Cloudy Bay
producers.why: Founded at Rapaura in 1985 by the owners of Margaret River's Cape Mentelle; its first vintage made Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc famous, and Te Koko and Pelorus followed.

producers.name: Brancott Estate
producers.why: The brand that was Montana, planter of the region's first commercial vines in 1973 and its first Sauvignon Blanc in 1975.

producers.name: Greywacke
producers.why: Founded 2009 by Cloudy Bay's founding winemaker, named after the valley's stone; the Wild Sauvignon is the model of the barrel-fermented school.

producers.name: Villa Maria
producers.why: The national house with large Marlborough holdings in the Wairau and Awatere and reserve wines from single vineyards.

producers.name: Dog Point
producers.why: Founded in the early 2000s by two Cloudy Bay veterans in the Southern Valleys; Section 94 Sauvignon Blanc and a serious Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Hunter's
producers.why: An estate of the early 1980s whose Sauvignon Blanc won in London in 1986 and told the world the region was real.

producers.name: Seresin
producers.why: An organic and biodynamic estate founded 1992, with vineyards in the Wairau and the Southern Valleys, making textured Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Fromm
producers.why: Founded 1992 with a European eye for Pinot Noir and Syrah from the clay of the Southern Valleys.

producers.name: Yealands
producers.why: The large Awatere estate of the 2000s whose cool coastal Sauvignon Blanc shows the valley's herbal, saline style.

producers.name: Te Whare Ra
producers.why: Some of the region's oldest vines, planted in 1979 at Renwick, farmed organically, with aromatic whites of long standing.

terroir.climate: Cool, dry and the sunniest region in New Zealand, with Blenheim regularly topping the national sunshine hours; the Richmond Range to the west takes the rain, so the Wairau sees around 650 millimetres a year and little of it in autumn. Warm days and cold nights hold acidity through a long hang. The Awatere is cooler, windier and drier again, and ripens a fortnight later.
terroir.soils: The Wairau floor is a braided river's leavings: greywacke gravel and stones near Rapaura and Renwick that drain at once and cut vigour, deeper silt loams towards the coast at Dillons Point that hold water and give the loudest, most tropical fruit. The Southern Valleys carry clay-bound loess over gravel, which suits Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. The Awatere's terraces are wind-blown loess and silt over gravel.
terroir.topography: Two valleys running east to the sea: the Wairau broad and flat between the Richmond Range and the Wither Hills, the Awatere narrower and higher beyond the Withers to the south. The Southern Valleys (Brancott, Omaka, Fairhall, Waihopai and Ben Morven) are the Wairau's side valleys on its southern flank. Blind River and the Kekerengu coast lie further south again.
terroir.water: The Wairau and Awatere rivers built their valleys and feed the aquifer that irrigates most of the Wairau; Cloudy Bay and Cook Strait bring the sea breeze that keeps the afternoons cool. Irrigation is almost universal on the stones, from the aquifer and from the Southern Valleys scheme.

traps: Marlborough has internal geography: the Awatere is cooler, greener and saline; the Wairau riper and tropical. One answer for both is wrong.
The sub-valleys are addresses, not GIs; Marlborough is the only registered name here.
Appellation Marlborough Wine is a growers' certification with a 100 per cent rule; the law's rule is 85 per cent.
Cloudy Bay (1985) was not the first; Montana planted in 1973 and made its first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc in 1979.
Machine harvesting here is a quality choice as much as a cost one: skin contact in the bin raises the thiol precursors.
The green notes are pyrazines, destroyed by sun; the tropical notes are thiols, released by yeast. The exam asks which is which.
Greywacke is both the valley's stone and a producer; the context tells which.

wines.note: Passionfruit, gooseberry, grapefruit and cut grass with a capsicum edge, bone dry or near it, high in acid, unoaked; serve well chilled and young with oysters, green salads, asparagus and goat's cheese.

Fermented with wild yeast in old barrels and left on lees: smoky, waxy and textured, the fruit toned down; Cloudy Bay's Te Koko, Greywacke's Wild Sauvignon and Dog Point's Section 94 are the models. Serve cool with richer fish and roast chicken.
Red cherry, raspberry and spice with soft tannin and fresh acidity, lighter than Martinborough's and Central Otago's; serve a touch cool with salmon, duck or pork.

Pinot Noir and Chardonnay bottle fermented, citrus and brioche with crisp acidity; the Deutz Marlborough Cuvée joint venture of 1988 and Cloudy Bay's Pelorus set the standard. An aperitif and a match for fried food.
Pear, apple and ginger, off-dry and gently textured; a crowd wine for pork, mild curries and smoked fish.
Apricot, marmalade and honey over lime acidity from fruit the fungus has reached in a damp autumn; a match for blue cheese and fruit tarts.

exam: Place Martinborough at the southern end of the Wairarapa, east of the Remutaka and Tararua ranges, an hour from Wellington.
Name Pinot Noir as the grape, 1979 and 1980 as the first plantings, and Ata Rangi, Dry River and Martinborough Vineyard as the founding houses.
Explain the terrace: thin silt over deep free-draining gravel, low rainfall in the rain shadow, the north-westerly that cuts the crop.
Describe the style: darker, firmer and more savoury than Central Otago, with small yields.
Know the three nested GIs, Wairarapa, Martinborough and Gladstone.
At Advanced, add Te Muna Road, the Abel clone and Dry River's long-lived whites.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The grape that made the town: dark cherry and plum with dried herb, earth and spice, firmer and more savoury than Central Otago's, from small wind-pruned crops on the terrace.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The wider Wairarapa's volume white, planted heavily around Gladstone and Masterton; riper and less pungent than Marlborough's, with stone fruit over the herbs.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Dry to off-dry and textured, a terrace speciality at Dry River and its followers.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Barrel fermented, taut and mineral in the cool dry season; a small, fine crop.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Dry to late harvest and, in the years the fungus comes, botrytised; long-lived on the terrace's acidity.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: A small crop from the warmest sites, peppery and perfumed in the Hawke's Bay manner, made by Dry River among others.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Aromatic and dry, a minor terrace planting of long standing.

law.classification: Three registered Geographical Indications nest here: Wairarapa for the whole valley, with Martinborough and Gladstone as local GIs inside it, all applied for when the register opened in July 2017. A label that names Martinborough must take 85 per cent of its grapes from the GI, and a wine from Te Muna Road or Masterton that wants a GI name uses Martinborough or Wairarapa. The Martinborough Terrace is a soil feature and a growers' phrase, not a boundary of law. No tier, yield or tasting panel exists; the hierarchy a server sees, Pinot Noir from the terrace above Sauvignon Blanc from the valley, is one of reputation.
labels: Wairarapa
The Māori name of the valley and its lake; also the regional GI that holds Martinborough and Gladstone.
Te Muna
The terrace district east of the town, planted from the late 1990s; a vineyard name on labels.
Martinborough Terrace
The growers' name for the gravel terrace around the town where the first vineyards were planted.
Abel clone
A Pinot Noir clone of uncertain origin used at several Martinborough houses, also called the Gumboot clone.
tiers: Wairarapa GI
The whole valley from Masterton to Palliser Bay; the name a blend across its districts carries.
Martinborough GI
The local GI around the town and its terraces, the one the famous Pinot Noir wears.
Gladstone GI
The local GI in the middle of the valley, around the Gladstone district east of Carterton.
The 85 per cent rule
Any of the three names needs that share of the grapes from inside it; the same for a stated grape or vintage.
Addresses
Martinborough Terrace, Te Muna Road, Masterton: vineyard descriptions without registration.

made.viticulture: The terrace was planted on the strength of a government soil survey of 1979 that found deep free-draining gravel, low rainfall and a heat summation near Burgundy's, and the first growers, from 1979 and 1980, planted Pinot Noir on it by hand. Yields are small because the soil gives little and the north-westerly strips flowers, so a Martinborough crop is far smaller than a Marlborough one; growers accept it, and the concentration is the style. Vines are trained to vertical shoot positioning, cane pruned, leaf plucked on the morning side and netted against birds; frost fans stand on the terrace. Clones matter here: the Abel clone, said to descend from a cutting seized at Auckland airport in the 1970s, gives the dark, spicy backbone at several houses alongside the Dijon clones and clone 10/5. Picking is by hand from late March into April, often in several passes. Rain is rare in autumn, so botrytis is a choice rather than a risk, and the houses that want it leave Riesling and Pinot Gris to hang. Sauvignon Blanc for the wider Wairarapa is grown on the valley loams at Gladstone and Masterton, much of it by machine.
made.winemaking: Pinot Noir is sorted, partly destemmed, with a quarter to a third whole bunches at the houses that like stem spice, cold soaked for a few days, fermented with wild yeast in open tanks with hand plunging, pressed and raised ten to sixteen months in French oak, a third or less new, then bottled under screwcap, often unfined and unfiltered. The result is darker and firmer than Central Otago's, cherry and plum with dried herb, earth and a savoury tannin that rewards five to ten years. Sauvignon Blanc is tank fermented and fresh; Chardonnay barrel fermented with partial malolactic; Pinot Gris made dry to off-dry with texture from lees. Dry River set the pattern of late-picked, long-lived whites and a botrytised Riesling in the years the fungus comes. Syrah, a small crop from the warmer sites, follows the Hawke's Bay model of pepper and perfume.

places.name: The Martinborough Terrace
places.note: The raised gravel terrace around the town, where the vineyards of 1979 and 1980 were planted on thin silt over deep free-draining stones; the home of Ata Rangi, Dry River and Martinborough Vineyard and of the region's reputation.

places.name: Te Muna Road
places.note: A higher, slightly cooler terrace a few kilometres east of the town above the Huangarua River, planted from the late 1990s by Escarpment and Craggy Range; later picking and a fresher, more floral Pinot Noir.

places.name: Gladstone
places.note: The district in the middle of the valley east of Carterton on loam over gravel, a registered local GI, with Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and aromatic whites from small estates.

places.name: Masterton
places.note: The valley's main town at its northern end and the district around it, on the fertile valley floor, where Sauvignon Blanc for volume and some Pinot Noir are grown.

places.name: The valley floor and Palliser Bay
places.note: The Ruamahanga's floodplain south of the town running to Lake Wairarapa and the open coast of Palliser Bay, where the wind off Cook Strait comes from; grazing land more than vineyard.

producers.name: Ata Rangi
producers.why: Founded 1980 on the terrace, the Martinborough name every sommelier knows, for a Pinot Noir of dark fruit, spice and long life built in large part on the Abel clone.

producers.name: Dry River
producers.why: Founded 1979, a tiny estate of famously low yields whose late-picked Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewürztraminer and Syrah are built for long ageing.

producers.name: Martinborough Vineyard
producers.why: Founded 1980; its Pinot Noirs of the late 1980s and early 1990s helped announce the region abroad.

producers.name: Palliser Estate
producers.why: Founded in the 1980s, one of the region's larger houses, with Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and traditional-method sparkling.

producers.name: Escarpment
producers.why: Founded 1998 on Te Muna Road by a pioneer of the terrace, with single-vineyard Pinot Noir and the flagship Kupe.

producers.name: Craggy Range
producers.why: The Hawke's Bay house whose Te Muna Road vineyard, planted from 1999, makes one of the district's best-known Pinot Noirs.

producers.name: Te Kairanga
producers.why: Founded in the 1980s, among the first and largest estates on the terrace, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay across several vineyards.

terroir.climate: Cool and dry in the rain shadow of the ranges, with some of the lowest rainfall on the North Island, a long dry autumn and cold nights that keep acidity. The north-westerly is the region's weather: it blows through flowering and shrinks the crop, and it dries the fruit against rot. Spring frost on the terrace is fought with wind machines.
terroir.soils: The Martinborough Terrace is a raised bed of old river gravel capped by a thin silt loam, free-draining for many metres, so the roots go deep and the vine's vigour stays low. The Te Muna Road terrace to the east is higher and a little cooler on similar gravels; Gladstone and Masterton carry more alluvial loam over gravel.
terroir.topography: The Wairarapa is a broad valley between the Tararua and Remutaka ranges on the west and the coastal hills on the east, running south to Palliser Bay and Cook Strait. Martinborough sits at its dry southern end on a terrace above the floodplain; Gladstone and Masterton lie north along the valley.
terroir.water: The Ruamahanga River and its tributary the Huangarua laid the terrace and bound it; Palliser Bay and Cook Strait lie to the south, and the valley is open to the wind. Rainfall is low enough that drip irrigation is common on the terrace.

traps: Martinborough is a town and a local GI inside the Wairarapa GI; the atlas writes both names, the register holds both.
Pinot Noir is the most planted grape of the whole Wairarapa, with Sauvignon Blanc second; the terrace is Pinot country and the valley loams grow both.
The Remutaka Range is on the road from Wellington; the Tararua Range runs north of it along the same western wall.
The style is savoury and firm, not the plush dark fruit of Central Otago; the two are the exam's favourite Pinot contrast.
Dry rather than cool is the region's mark: rainfall is low, the autumn is dry and botrytis is a choice.
Te Muna Road is a terrace district with no GI of its own; its wines say Martinborough.

wines.note: Dark cherry, plum, dried thyme and earth with a firm, savoury tannin and fresh acidity, medium-bodied; it rewards five to ten years and suits duck, lamb and mushroom dishes. Serve a touch below room temperature.
Gooseberry and white peach over a gentler herbal note than Marlborough's, dry and fresh; a wine for shellfish, green salads and goat's cheese, drunk young.
Pear, quince and spice with a textured, off-dry palate in the Alsace manner; it carries pork, smoked fish and mild curries.
Citrus and white peach with a flinty edge and lively acidity from barrel fermentation; serve cool with chicken, crab or a cream sauce.
Apricot, honey and lime with piercing acidity, made only in the years the dry autumn allows the fungus; a match for blue cheese and fruit tarts.
wines.style: Martinborough late harvest and botrytised Riesling

exam: Place Nelson on Tasman Bay at the top of the South Island, west of Marlborough across the Richmond Range.
Name the two districts and their soils: Waimea Plains on young stony alluvium, Moutere Hills on weathered clay gravel.
Give the grapes: Sauvignon Blanc most planted, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay the fine wines, Riesling and Gewürztraminer the aromatic calling card.
Know Neudorf (1978) as the house and Moutere Chardonnay as the wine, and 1973 as the first modern planting.
Explain the climate: as sunny as Marlborough, wetter, with autumn rain the hazard.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The most planted grape, grown on the plains in the Marlborough way but riper and rounder for the warmer, wetter season.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Soft, perfumed and red-fruited from the plains, denser and more savoury from the Moutere clay.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The region's finest wine from the Moutere Hills: textured, long and mineral, barrel fermented with wild yeast, built to age.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Pear and spice, off-dry and textured, a large crop on the plains.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Lime, apple and honeysuckle, dry to late harvest, the aromatic the region is proudest of.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Lychee and rose, dry to off-dry, a long-standing Nelson speciality.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: A recent planting on the plains that suits the sunny, damp coast.

law.classification: Nelson is a registered Geographical Indication, applied for when the register opened in July 2017, with the one national rule: 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the line, and 85 per cent for a stated grape or vintage. Nothing below it is registered; Moutere Hills, Upper Moutere, Waimea Plains and Brightwater are growers' names and vineyard addresses, and a wine from the hills may say so only as a vineyard description. The region has no private appellation scheme of the Marlborough kind. Organic and biodynamic claims rest on BioGro and Demeter certification, and the national sustainability programme certifies the great majority of vineyards. Styles, tiers and yields are a house's choice.
labels: Moutere
The clay hills west of the plains; Upper Moutere is the village and the heart of the hill vineyards.
Waimea
The plains and river south-west of the city, the region's flat, stony vineyard land.
Tasman
The bay the region faces and the district that holds most of its vineyards.
Sarau
The German settlers' name of the 1840s for Upper Moutere, kept by the village's festival.
tiers: New Zealand (GI)
The national origin; a Nelson wine blended with Marlborough fruit falls back to it.
Nelson GI
The regional name, applied for in the first intake of 2017; 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the boundary.
District names
Moutere Hills, Upper Moutere, Waimea Plains, Brightwater, Motueka: addresses and growers' terms, with no registered GI of their own.
Certification
BioGro organic and Demeter biodynamic seals are private; SWNZ is the industry's sustainability programme.

made.viticulture: The plains are farmed much as Marlborough's floor is: vertical shoot positioning, cane pruning, drip irrigation on the stones and machine harvest for the larger houses, with crops kept moderate because the autumn can turn wet. The Moutere Hills are a different trade: close-planted vines on north-facing clay slopes, dry farmed or nearly so, cropped low, hand picked and tended by estates small enough to pick in a day when rain threatens. Botrytis and downy mildew are the standing threats, so canopies are open and leaf plucked, and harvest timing is a judgement about the forecast as much as about sugar. Riesling and Gewürztraminer like the cool bright autumn and are left to hang for aromatic ripeness when the weather allows; a botrytised Riesling is a possibility rather than a plan. Hops, apples and orchards share the land, which tells a server the climate: sunny, fertile and wetter than the stony east. Organic farming is well established on the hills. The first modern vineyard was planted at Upper Moutere in 1973 and the region's best-known estate followed at the same village in 1978.
made.winemaking: Chardonnay from the Moutere is barrel fermented with wild yeast, left on lees with little or no stirring and a partial malolactic, held a year in French oak with a modest share new, and bottled to age: the style is textured and long rather than fruity. Pinot Noir is partly whole bunch, wild fermented in open vats, pressed to French oak for ten to twelve months, and comes out softer and more perfumed than Martinborough's. The aromatic whites are picked at full flavour, pressed gently, fermented cool in tank and stopped with a little residual sugar when the acidity asks for it; Gewürztraminer is given a short skin soak for texture, and Riesling runs from bone dry to late harvest. Sauvignon Blanc is made in the Marlborough way, cool and reductive in stainless steel, and tastes riper and rounder for the warmer, wetter season. Screwcap is standard.

places.name: Moutere Hills
places.note: The rolling hills between the Waimea Plains and Motueka on ancient weathered clay gravels that hold water and give low yields; the home of the region's Chardonnay and Pinot Noir and of its most famous estates.

places.name: Upper Moutere
places.note: The village at the heart of the hills, settled by Germans in the 1840s, where the first modern vines were planted in 1973 and Neudorf followed in 1978.

places.name: Mahana
places.note: A locality near Upper Moutere and the name of a hill estate with a gravity-fed winery.

places.name: Waimea Plains
places.note: The flat alluvial land south-west of Nelson city around Richmond, Brightwater and Hope, stony and free-draining, where Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling and most of the region's volume are grown with drip irrigation.

places.name: Brightwater
places.note: The township on the plains south of Richmond with several estates on the river gravels; Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Hope
places.note: The locality on the plains between Richmond and Brightwater where some of the region's early Pinot Noir and Riesling estates were planted.

places.name: Motueka and the north
places.note: The hop and orchard country at the northern end of the Moutere towards the Abel Tasman coast, with small plantings on the river flats.

producers.name: Neudorf
producers.why: Founded 1978 at Upper Moutere; its Moutere Chardonnay is the wine that gave Nelson a place among the country's best, with Pinot Noir and Riesling beside it.

producers.name: Seifried Estate
producers.why: The modern region's founding family, planting at Upper Moutere in 1973 and long its largest house, with Riesling, Gewürztraminer and a sweet Riesling of long standing.

producers.name: Greenhough
producers.why: A Hope estate on the plains known for Pinot Noir and Riesling, farmed organically.

producers.name: Kahurangi Estate
producers.why: An Upper Moutere estate on the site of the region's first modern vineyard, with Riesling and aromatic whites from some of its oldest vines.

producers.name: Brightwater Vineyards
producers.why: A family estate on the Waimea gravels making Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and Pinot Noir in the plains style.

producers.name: Mahana
producers.why: The hill estate near Upper Moutere, formerly Woollaston, with a gravity-fed winery and organic Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
