terroir.climate: Cool maritime and among the sunniest places in the country, rivalling Blenheim, but wetter: around a metre of rain a year, some of it in autumn, so vintage can be a race against the weather. The mountains to the west and south shelter it from the worst of the westerlies, and the bay moderates both frost and heat.
terroir.soils: Two soils make two wines. The Waimea Plains are young, stony alluvial soils from the Waimea and Wairoa rivers, free-draining and warm, farmed much like the Wairau. The Moutere Hills are an ancient gravel formation weathered into clay, deep and water-holding with low fertility, which gives small crops and dense fruit.
terroir.topography: An amphitheatre of plains and low hills opening north onto Tasman Bay, with the Richmond Range to the east, the Arthur Range and the Kahurangi mountains to the west and the Moutere's rolling clay hills between the plains and Motueka. Vineyards sit on the flats around Richmond and Brightwater and on the north-facing Moutere slopes.
terroir.water: Tasman Bay keeps the climate even; the Waimea and Motueka rivers built the plains. Rain is generous enough that the hill vineyards need little irrigation, while the stony plains use drip water in a dry summer.

traps: Nelson is as sunny as Marlborough but wetter; sunshine does not mean dryness here.
Moutere is clay and hills, Waimea is stones and plains; the exam asks which gives the Chardonnay (Moutere).
Sauvignon Blanc is the most planted grape, but the region's reputation rests on aromatics, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Nelson is west of Marlborough, not south; the Richmond Range stands between them.
Tasman Bay is Nelson's water; Golden Bay lies further west, Cloudy Bay is Marlborough's.

wines.note: Grapefruit, white peach and a stony, savoury length with a creamy lees texture and restrained oak; serve cool with crayfish, scallops or roast chicken. The best keep ten years.
Red cherry, raspberry and a floral lift with soft tannin, fuller and earthier from the Moutere clay; serve a touch cool with duck, salmon or mushroom dishes.
Lime, green apple and honeysuckle over bright acidity, dry to off-dry, with a late harvest version in the right year; a match for Asian dishes, pork and fresh cheeses.
Lychee, rose and ginger, oily and usually just off-dry; a wine for spiced food and washed-rind cheese.
Riper and softer than Marlborough's, passionfruit and stone fruit over a gentler herbal edge; drink young and cold with shellfish and salads.

exam: Give the shape of the country: maritime everywhere but Central Otago, vineyards east of the Alps, strong light, cool nights, rot the hazard.
Know the 85 per cent rule for region, variety and vintage, and that a GI is origin only.
Date the GI law: the Act of 2006, in force 27 July 2017, the first registrations from 2018, North Canterbury 2020, Bannockburn 2022.
Place the four regions the exam asks hardest: Marlborough, Central Otago, Hawke's Bay and Martinborough, each with its grape.
Name the milestones: Mission Estate 1851, Montana in Marlborough 1973, Cloudy Bay 1985, the Screwcap Initiative 2001.
Be ready for the chemistry: pyrazines green and sun-sensitive, thiols tropical and yeast-released.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The national grape by a distance: pungent, dry, unoaked and screwcapped, passionfruit and gooseberry over cut grass and capsicum, nearly all of it from Marlborough.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The leading red and the sparkling base, from the dark, generous wines of Central Otago to the savoury ones of Martinborough and the lighter Marlborough style.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown in every region; barrel fermented and Burgundian in Kumeu and Hawke's Bay, ripe and peachy in Gisborne, taut in Marlborough.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: The fourth grape, made in the Alsace manner, off-dry and textured, especially in the South Island.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Dry to botrytised in Waipara, Nelson, Marlborough and Central Otago, taut and long-lived.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted Bordeaux grape, leading the Hawke's Bay blends because it ripens before Cabernet Sauvignon.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Small in area, large in reputation: cool-climate Syrah of white pepper and violets from the Gimblett Gravels and Waiheke Island.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripens reliably only in the warmest spots, the Hawke's Bay gravels and Waiheke Island; leads a blend in a warm year, supports Merlot in a cool one.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Lychee and rose, oily and usually just off-dry, a Gisborne and Nelson speciality.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: A new arrival that suits the wet coast, saline and fresh, planted in Gisborne, Marlborough and Hawke's Bay.

labels: GI
Geographical Indication: a registered origin, with nothing to say on grape, style or yield.
Méthode Traditionnelle
Bottle-fermented sparkling wine; Méthode Marlborough is a trade group's mark for that region's version.
Single Vineyard
From one named vineyard; a claim of truth, lightly policed.
Late Harvest, Botrytis, Noble
Sweet wine terms; New Zealand sets no must-weight ladder behind them.
Appellation Marlborough Wine
A growers' certification from 2018: every grape from Marlborough, bottled in New Zealand, from sustainably certified vineyards.
SWNZ
Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand, the industry programme that certifies the great majority of vineyards.
Aotearoa
The Māori name for New Zealand, seen on labels and in the trade.
Syrah
New Zealand labels almost always say Syrah rather than Shiraz, a signal that the style is cool, peppery and Rhône-leaning.
ladder: The national name, protected by the Act itself alongside North Island and South Island; a blend across regions carries it, with 85 per cent of the grapes grown in the country.

Northland, Auckland, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Wairarapa, Marlborough, Nelson, Canterbury, Central Otago and Waitaki Valley North Otago: the names a label carries, applied for when the register opened in 2017 and registered from 2018.

A registered name inside a region: Matakana, Kumeu and Waiheke Island in Auckland, Central Hawke's Bay in Hawke's Bay (2019), Martinborough and Gladstone in the Wairarapa, North Canterbury (2020) and Waipara Valley in Canterbury, Bannockburn in Central Otago (2022).
A stated GI, grape or vintage must make up at least 85 per cent of the wine; the rule sits in the wine labelling rules, not in the GI Act.
Gimblett Gravels (a trademark on a soil boundary, 2001), Appellation Marlborough Wine (2018), Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand, BioGro and Demeter: none is a tier of law.
A producer's words, held only to being true; no yield, panel or ranking stands behind them.
new-zealand.overview:
Vines came with the missionaries. Samuel Marsden planted them at Kerikeri in 1819, James Busby was making wine at Waitangi by 1840, and the Marist fathers founded the house that became Mission Estate in Hawke's Bay in 1851. The government viticulturist Romeo Bragato reported in 1895 that the country could make fine wine, and in the same year phylloxera was found. Dalmatian settlers around Auckland kept wine alive through decades of temperance law, hybrid grapes and fortified wine; restaurants could not sell wine until 1960 and supermarkets until 1990. The vineyard of the 1970s was Müller-Thurgau. Montana planted Marlborough in 1973 and Sauvignon Blanc there in 1975, a government vine pull in 1986 cleared much of the bulk planting, and the fame of Cloudy Bay's first vintage in 1985 made Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc the country's calling card within a decade.

The vineyards run from about 35°S in Northland to about 45°S in Central Otago, and the Southern Alps wring the westerlies dry, so every South Island vineyard lies to their east. The sea moderates the summers and cools the nights, ultraviolet light is strong, and the growing season is often wet, which makes open canopies and spray timing the grower's year. Only Central Otago, inland behind the mountains, is continental. Phylloxera is present and most vines are grafted. The industry's answers have been its own: machine harvest at scale, Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand from the mid 1990s, and the Screwcap Initiative of 2001, after which nearly the whole range, fine wine included, went under screwcap.

The law is light. The Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006 came into force on 27 July 2017 after a 2016 amendment. Applications went in that day and the Intellectual Property Office registered the names over the following years, Hawke's Bay among the first in February 2018: the regions themselves and a few places inside them such as Martinborough, Gladstone, Matakana, Kumeu, Waiheke Island, Waipara Valley and Central Hawke's Bay, while New Zealand, North Island and South Island are names the Act itself protects. North Canterbury was registered on 29 June 2020 and Bannockburn, inside Central Otago, on 1 February 2022. A GI draws a boundary and nothing else: no grape list, no yield, no tasting panel. A stated region, variety or vintage must account for 85 per cent of the wine. Everything above that floor is private: the Gimblett Gravels is a trademarked district drawn on a soil boundary, Appellation Marlborough Wine is a growers' certification from 2018, and estate, reserve and single vineyard are claims the producer makes.

The exam leans on Marlborough's Sauvignon Blanc and its two valleys, Central Otago's continental Pinot Noir, Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels with Syrah and Merlot blends, Martinborough's Pinot Noir, the 85 per cent rule, the GI register and the screwcap. Behind those sit Gisborne's Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer, Nelson's aromatic whites, Waipara's Riesling, Kumeu's Chardonnay and the Bordeaux blends of Waiheke Island off Auckland.

Central Otago is the continental exception; calling the whole country maritime is a loose but common error.
Latitude misleads: Blenheim lies as far south as Rome lies north, and shares nothing else with it.
New Zealand Syrah is cool and peppery, nearer the northern Rhône than Barossa; Shiraz on a label usually signals Australia.
